transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [name]. Well, I'm here because things at work are getting pretty bad. I'm a maintenance worker, and lately, I just keep forgetting things. I'm missing scheduled callbacks, misplacing work orders, and forgetting basic follow-ups I promised people. It's just piled up so much that my boss actually told me I needed to come see someone. I'm up for a promotion, and they basically said I need to get this sorted out before I lose my shot at moving up.
Have you struggled with this kind of forgetfulness and distractibility since childhood, or is this a new problem that started recently?

No, it's not new at all. I remember being exactly like this back in grade school, honestly, long before any of this job pressure started. Um, my teachers used to say I was bright, but I was just always misplacing my papers. I'd miss parts of the directions when they explained things, and they constantly had to give me reminders just to finish my regular classwork. So, yeah, it's been going on since I was a kid.

latest_inference.note: Childhood-onset inattentiveness, distractibility, and disorganization strongly support ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. This rules out F32.9, F41.1, F43.20, and F06.7, which typically involve later onset or mood/anxiety/cognitive decline patterns not consistent with a lifelong trait history.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a long-standing pattern of inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, disorganization, losing materials, missing details, difficulty completing tasks without reminders) that began in childhood (grade school) and has persisted into adulthood, now causing significant occupational impairment (missed callbacks, misplaced work orders, jeopardized promotion). The chronicity since childhood, cross-situational presence (school and work), and functional impairment support a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation (F90.0). No evidence of psychotic, mood, or acute stressor-related symptoms to better explain the presentation.
